    YOUR POCKET FIELD GUIDE

    Rows, hidden colors, and surprises.

    One jar fills one row

    There are six separate populations of eight beetles. Drag two living beetles into a row’s jar, or select a beetle and click an empty slot. Press that jar’s Breed row button to replace only its eight beetles. Empty and unfinished jars leave their rows unchanged. Breed ready rows breeds all complete jars together. Each row has its own generation count; the round counter counts steps in the experiment.

    Parents may come from any row. You may reuse a parent across jars, but a pair needs two different beetles. After breeding, references to parents no longer living on the board are cleared. Use pair in all jars explicitly prepares all six rows.

    Visible colors and hidden alleles

    Each beetle carries two versions (alleles) of a color gene, one from each parent. In this teaching model, Green (G) masks Yellow (Y), Blue (B), and Red (R); Yellow masks Blue and Red; Blue masks Red. The masked allele is still present and can be passed on. Dominance decides which color shows; it does not make that color better at surviving.

    For example, a G/B beetle looks green but carries blue. Crossing G/B × G/B gives four equally likely combinations: G/G, G/B, B/G, B/B. Each baby has a 75% chance to show green and 25% to show blue, before mutation. Eight babies are independent draws, so exactly two blue babies are not guaranteed. Use Try a carrier cross to select two living green/blue carriers and set mutation to 0%.

    Can yellow or red appear randomly?

    Yes. Offspring randomly inherit existing color alleles, so hidden yellow or red may reappear. Mutations are a separate source of surprises: a transmitted color allele may randomly change to any of the other three colors. The change can be visible immediately or carried hidden. Mutations do not aim for the background color. With mutation at 0%, offspring can only inherit alleles already carried by their parents.

    Three additional shade genes make beetles slightly lighter, darker, or different in tone. Each has two numeric copies, and a baby gets one copy per parent. The advanced preview enumerates 4 color transmissions × 4 × 4 × 4 shade transmissions = 256 equally likely combinations before mutation. Color probabilities are grouped by the visible color family; shades may differ.

    The mutation slider applies independently to eight inherited copies: two color alleles and six shade copies. A color mutation changes to another color allele. A shade mutation shifts a value up or down by 1–36, within 0–255. Pale dots mark offspring with any mutation; the inspector and data export distinguish color-allele mutations.

    The bird and natural selection

    In natural mode, the bird eats four non-survivors in each row. Camouflaged beetles have better survival odds, but chance still matters. That row’s four survivors produce its next eight beetles. There is no automatic mixing between rows. At 0% selection, survival is random. The bird displays the already-selected outcome. Turn off its animation to shorten the transition; reduced-motion settings also skip the moving bird.

    Try an experiment

    1. Try the carrier cross at 0% mutation and predict the babies.
    2. Breed just row 1. Check that rows 2–6 keep their beetles and generation counters.
    3. Inspect a green, yellow, blue, or red beetle to discover the allele it carries.
    4. Raise mutation and compare inherited surprises with new color-allele mutations.
    5. Try natural selection in a new habitat and compare the separate rows.

    Reading the results

    Average camouflage is a 0–100% similarity score, not a survival probability. Diversity measures color spread. The chart summarizes all six rows after each round; row generations can differ. Changing the habitat immediately changes camouflage, but never recolors existing beetles.

    A teaching model

    Real beetle coloration is more complex. This invented four-allele hierarchy, independent shade genes, fixed row sizes, and camouflage-only selection illustrate inheritance, dominance, recessive carriers, mutation, and genetic drift. They are not a claim about actual beetle color genetics. Learn more about recessive alleles and dominant alleles from NHGRI.

    Use a mouse, trackpad, pen, or touch to drag. With a keyboard, select a beetle then activate an empty jar slot. On small screens, swipe along a row. Save data downloads row generations, carried alleles, parentage, mutation counts, and your notes. No account is needed to play.
